project.name: lunchbox
project.description: Office lunch orders. Built in a weekend with an AI assistant. A deliberately flawed example for Readback.
project.readmeLine: Lunchbox lets an office order lunch together, pay in one go, and get a meal suggestion from AI.

run.name: dev
run.plain: Starts the app on your own computer for development.

run.name: start
run.plain: Starts the built app, the way a server would.

stack.name: Next.js
stack.plain: A framework built on React. It decides which code runs in the browser and which runs on your server, and it turns your folders into website addresses.
stack.analogy: The building your app lives in: it already has the wiring, so you only add the rooms.

stack.name: React
stack.plain: A library for building screens out of small reusable pieces called components. When data changes, React redraws only the pieces that need it.

stack.name: Supabase
stack.plain: A hosted Postgres database with login, file storage and an API on top. Your browser can talk to it directly, so its access rules are the only thing standing between strangers and your data.

stack.name: OpenAI
stack.plain: Sends text to a model like GPT and returns what it wrote. You pay per word, so each call costs money, and the text you send leaves your server.

stack.name: TypeScript
stack.plain: JavaScript with labels saying what kind of data each thing is. Mistakes show up before the code runs. Browsers never see it: it is converted to JavaScript first.

stack.name: Tailwind CSS
stack.plain: Styling through short class names written directly on each element, instead of separate CSS files.

stack.name: Stripe
stack.plain: Takes card payments for you. Your app never sees card numbers. Stripe tells your server what happened through webhooks.

stack.name: Zod
stack.plain: Checks that data has the shape you expect before your code uses it. Anything arriving from outside should go through something like this.

risks.title: 2 routes change data and I can see no login check
risks.why: These are doors on the internet. If nothing checks who is knocking, anyone who finds the address can change your data, with no need for your app.
risks.check: Open a private browser window with no login and send the request. Does it work?
risks.caveat: If this app only ever runs on your own computer, or a proxy or helper I could not follow protects it, this is a false alarm. Decide by testing, not by assuming.
risks.fixPrompt:
These routes change data with no visible login check:
- DELETE /api/orders/:id (app/api/orders/[id]/route.ts:5)
- POST /api/orders (app/api/orders/route.ts:9)

For each one, tell me who should be allowed to call it. Then add a check at the top of the handler that returns 401 when nobody is logged in and 403 when the user does not own the record. Do not change anything else.

risks.title: Anyone can make you pay: POST /api/suggest spends AI credit with no login check
risks.why: Every call to this route costs you real money. A simple loop from one stranger could run up your bill overnight.
risks.check: Set a hard spending limit on your AI provider today. Then look at whether this route needs a login or a rate limit.
risks.caveat: I recognise common rate limit names and packages. A limit with an unusual name, or one set at your host, would not show up here.
risks.fixPrompt: POST /api/suggest call a paid AI model and have no login check. Add a per-user or per-IP rate limit, and cap the size of the input. Show me what the limit is before you add it.

risks.title: 2 tables have no row level security in your migrations
risks.why: Supabase gives your browser a public key on purpose. Row level security is what stops that key reading or changing everyone else's rows. Without it, your public key is a master key.
risks.check: Open the Supabase dashboard, go to Authentication then Policies, and look for tables marked RLS disabled.
risks.caveat: I only read migration files in this repository. RLS turned on by hand in the dashboard does not show up here.
risks.fixPrompt: Write a migration that enables row level security on: orders, profiles. Then propose a policy per table so each user can only see and change their own rows, and explain each one in a sentence.

risks.title: POST /api/stripe/webhook accepts webhooks and I cannot see it checking a signature
risks.why: A webhook address is public. Without checking the signature, anyone can send a fake "payment succeeded" and your app will believe it.
risks.check: Look for constructEvent, verifySignature or a comparison against a signing secret in this handler.
risks.caveat: I look for common names only, so a custom check could be missed.
risks.fixPrompt: Add signature verification to /api/stripe/webhook (app/api/stripe/webhook/route.ts) using the provider's official method, and reject anything that fails with a 400 before doing any work.

risks.title: .gitignore does not list .env
risks.why: Your code reads secrets from the environment, and nothing stops a future .env file being committed by accident.

risks.title: The browser writes directly to Supabase
risks.why: There is no server of yours in the middle, so your database's own access rules are the only check. Anything your screen can do, a visitor can do from their browser console.
risks.check: Confirm every table touched here has rules that limit people to their own rows.
risks.fixPrompt:
These browser calls write straight to Supabase:
- app/account/page.tsx:13
Check the access rules that cover each one and tell me whether a logged-in user could change someone else's data.

risks.title: Raw HTML is inserted into the page
risks.why: If that HTML contains anything a person typed, or anything a model wrote, it can run as code in other people's browsers and steal their sessions.
risks.check: Trace where the HTML comes from. If it is your own static text, this is fine.
risks.fixPrompt:
For each of these, either render as plain text, or sanitise with DOMPurify first:
- app/account/page.tsx:24

risks.title: 2 routes save incoming data without checking its shape
risks.why: TypeScript types disappear when the app runs. Whatever arrives over the network is exactly what the sender chose to send, including extra fields or the wrong kind of data.
risks.check: Send a request with a missing field and an extra field. What ends up in the database?
risks.caveat: I recognise Zod, Joi, Yup, Valibot and handwritten schema.parse calls. Manual if-checks are not counted.
risks.fixPrompt:
Add a Zod schema to validate the input of:
- DELETE /api/orders/:id (app/api/orders/[id]/route.ts)
- POST /api/orders (app/api/orders/route.ts)
Return a 400 with a clear message when it fails.
